ideas.title: Support for quitting
ideas.message: Quitting smoking helps health at any age. When you feel ready, you could call 1-800-QUIT-NOW for free, friendly support.
ideas.why: Support is there whenever you feel ready to quit.

ideas.title: The ten-minute delay
ideas.message: When a craving hits, tell yourself you'll wait ten minutes first. Set a timer, sip some water or step outside, and see if the urge fades. Each wait is good practice.
ideas.why: Most cravings pass if you can wait a little.

ideas.title: Swap the after-dinner cigarette
ideas.message: If you usually smoke after dinner, try a short stroll around the block instead, or out to the mailbox and back. A new after-meal habit fills the gap the cigarette leaves.
ideas.why: Swapping in a new habit is easier than just stopping.

ideas.title: Keep your hands busy
ideas.message: Keep something for your hands and mouth close by: a toothpick, sugar-free gum, crunchy carrot sticks or a stress ball. Reach for it when you'd usually reach for a cigarette.
ideas.why: A ready swap makes a craving easier to ride out.

ideas.title: Breathe through a craving
ideas.message: When a craving comes, try slow breathing: in through your nose while you count to four, out through your mouth while you count to six. A few rounds can take the edge off the urge.
ideas.why: Slow breathing gives a craving time to pass.

ideas.title: Tell someone you trust
ideas.message: Tell a friend or someone in your family that you're thinking about quitting, and ask if you can text them when a craving gets hard. Having someone in your corner can make the tough moments easier.
ideas.why: Quitting is easier with someone cheering you on.

ideas.title: Spot your triggers
ideas.message: For a couple of days, jot down when you light up: with coffee, in the car, after meals, on breaks. Knowing your triggers helps you plan a swap for each one.
ideas.why: Knowing when cravings come helps you plan for them.

ideas.title: A smoke-free car
ideas.message: If you smoke while driving, make the car a smoke-free zone. Clean out the ashtray, add a fresh air freshener and keep gum and a good playlist ready for the drive.
ideas.why: A smoke-free car takes away a driving trigger.

ideas.title: A smoke-free home
ideas.message: Make your home smoke-free, one room at a time or all at once. Stepping outside adds a pause that gives you a moment to choose, and it keeps the air fresh for the people and pets you love.
ideas.why: A pause before each cigarette gives you a choice.

ideas.title: Delay the first one
ideas.message: If your first cigarette comes with your morning coffee, try pushing it back a little each day: after your shower, then after breakfast. Shrinking the habit step by step still counts.
ideas.why: Small steps away from the habit still count.

ideas.title: A quit jar
ideas.message: Put the money you'd spend on cigarettes into a jar each day and watch it grow. Pick something you'd love to spend it on, like a meal out with friends or a gift for someone special.
ideas.why: Seeing your savings keeps your reason to quit close.

ideas.title: Ask about quit aids
ideas.message: Your doctor or pharmacist can talk you through quit aids such as the patch or gum, and which would suit you. You could bring it up at your next visit.
ideas.why: Quit aids and advice can make quitting easier.

ideas.title: A walk after meals
ideas.message: You could start small, with a short walk after a meal a few days a week.
ideas.why: A short, easy walk is a great place to begin.

ideas.title: Kettle dance
ideas.message: Put on three songs you love and dance around the kitchen while the kettle boils and the tea brews. No steps to learn, just move however feels good.
ideas.why: Moving to music you love hardly feels like exercise.

ideas.title: Dancing in your chair
ideas.message: Pick a favorite song and move from your chair: swing your arms, tap your feet and roll your shoulders. When it ends, play another.
ideas.why: Moving in your chair counts, and it's gentle.

ideas.title: A grocery store lap
ideas.message: Next time you shop, walk one easy lap of the grocery store before you start filling your cart. It's flat and dry, and the cart is there to lean on.
ideas.why: A walk folded into errands is easy to keep.

ideas.title: A walk-and-talk call
ideas.message: Call a friend or someone in your family and take a gentle stroll while you chat, around the block or even around the house. The time flies when you're catching up.
ideas.why: A good chat makes a walk fly by.

ideas.title: There and back
ideas.message: Pick a landmark close to home, like the mailbox, the corner or a neighbor's gate, and walk there and back. Go a little farther whenever it feels easy.
ideas.why: A short, familiar route is an easy first step.

ideas.title: Steps during your show
ideas.message: During one TV show, stand up and walk around the room whenever the ads come on. You'll be moving without missing a moment.
ideas.why: Moving during a favorite show makes it stick.

ideas.title: Park time with grandkids
ideas.message: Take the grandkids to the park and join in: push the swings, stroll the paths and chase a ball now and then. Their energy is catching.
ideas.why: Playing with grandkids hardly feels like exercise.

ideas.title: Garden minutes
ideas.message: Spend a little time in the garden: pull a few weeds, water the pots or rake a corner. Light garden work is real activity.
ideas.why: Garden jobs you enjoy count as activity.

ideas.title: Yes to the dog
ideas.message: Next time your dog asks to go out, take a slow stroll around the block together instead of just opening the door.
ideas.why: Your dog is a ready-made walking buddy.

ideas.title: Water-bottle lifts
ideas.message: Sit tall in a sturdy chair, hold a water bottle in each hand and raise your arms out to the sides, then lower them slowly. It's an easy one to do during the news.
ideas.why: Gentle seated moves are a kind way to begin.

ideas.title: A community stroll
ideas.message: Arrive at church or your community group a little early and take a gentle walk around the building or the grounds with someone you know.
ideas.why: A walk with friendly faces is easy to enjoy.

ideas.title: Walk in the pool
ideas.message: If you can get to a pool, walk back and forth in the shallow end. The water supports your joints, so it's a kind way to begin.
ideas.why: Water takes the strain off sore joints.

ideas.title: A slow morning loop
ideas.message: Start the day with an easy walk around the block or the garden, then come back to your coffee. A gentle, regular start is easy to keep.
ideas.why: Part of your morning, so there's nothing to remember.

ideas.title: A seated routine
ideas.message: In a sturdy chair, lift each knee in turn, circle your arms, and press your palms together, a few minutes of each, to music you like.
ideas.why: Moving in your chair counts, and it's gentle.

ideas.title: One more weekly session
ideas.message: Adding one more session a week of something you already enjoy is an easy way to build on it.
ideas.why: Building on what you enjoy is easier to keep up.

ideas.title: A new dog route
ideas.message: Take your dog a different, slightly longer way around. New smells for them, new sights for you, and a few extra minutes for both of you.
ideas.why: A new route makes a familiar walk fun again.

ideas.title: An extra dog walk
ideas.message: Add a short evening stroll with your dog on top of the usual walk. It's a calm way to end the day, for both of you.
ideas.why: Your dog is a ready-made walking buddy.

ideas.title: An adventure walk
ideas.message: Plan a little adventure walk with the grandkids: a nature trail, a scavenger hunt for leaves and stones, or a stroll to the ice cream shop.
ideas.why: Exploring with the grandkids turns a walk into an outing.

ideas.title: Park a little farther
ideas.message: When you drive somewhere, park at the far end of the lot and enjoy the extra stroll to the door and back.
ideas.why: Small extra walks fit into the day without a plan.

ideas.title: A lunchtime loop
ideas.message: Take a short walk on your lunch break or after lunch, even just around the building. A regular slot makes it easier to remember.
ideas.why: A regular slot makes a walk easy to remember.

ideas.title: Join a walking group
ideas.message: Look for a walking group at a community center, library or church. Walking with others makes it social, and they'll notice when you're missing.
ideas.why: Walking with others is social and easy to keep.

ideas.title: A dance night
ideas.message: Try a dance class or a social dance night: line dancing, ballroom or salsa. Many welcome beginners, and it hardly feels like exercise.
ideas.why: Dancing with others hardly feels like exercise.

ideas.title: An easy bike ride
ideas.message: Take your bike out for an easy ride on a flat path or a quiet street, or pedal an exercise bike while you watch something.
ideas.why: An easy ride gently adds a little activity.

ideas.title: Pool time
ideas.message: Add a swim or a pool walk to your week. Water takes the strain off your joints, so it's a gentle way to do a bit extra.
ideas.why: Water takes the strain off sore joints.

ideas.title: A longer garden session
ideas.message: Give the garden one extra session a week: mowing, digging a bed or raking leaves all count. Take breaks and switch tasks often.
ideas.why: Garden jobs you enjoy count as activity.

ideas.title: Walk with a story
ideas.message: Save a podcast, an audiobook or a favorite album just for walks. You'll look forward to the next chapter, and to the walk that comes with it.
ideas.why: Something to look forward to gets you out walking.

ideas.title: Mall walking
ideas.message: On rainy or cold days, walk laps of a mall or a big store. It's flat, has benches to rest on, and some open early for walkers.
ideas.why: Walking indoors keeps you going whatever the weather.

ideas.title: A gentle class
ideas.message: Look for a gentle exercise class at a community or senior center, like chair yoga or a seated exercise group. Many are made for beginners.
ideas.why: A class made for beginners takes the guesswork out.

ideas.title: Lamppost intervals
ideas.message: On your next walk, pick up the pace between two lampposts, then ease off for the next two, and keep swapping. Brisk bits that leave you a little out of breath count double.
ideas.why: Faster stretches are a simple next step for walkers.

ideas.title: Find a hill
ideas.message: Add a hill or a slope to your usual route and climb it at a steady push. Walking uphill turns an easy walk into a livelier one.
ideas.why: A hill adds effort to your usual walk.

ideas.title: Walk to the beat
ideas.message: Make a playlist of upbeat songs and match your steps to the beat for a song or two, then cool off with a slower one.
ideas.why: A quick beat makes a faster pace feel easy.

ideas.title: Race your dog home
ideas.message: For the last stretch of your dog walk, pick up the pace and let your dog set a quick tempo home. Brisk minutes like these count double.
ideas.why: Your dog is happy to set a quicker pace.

ideas.title: Tag with the grandkids
ideas.message: Join the grandkids in a game of tag or kick a ball around the yard. Short bursts of running around are the kind of activity that leaves you out of breath.
ideas.why: Running games with grandkids are lively, fun activity.

ideas.title: Take the stairs
ideas.message: Choose the stairs over the elevator when you can, and take them at a good pace. A couple of flights gets your heart going.
ideas.why: Stairs add quick effort to your day.

ideas.title: Brisk walks with friends
ideas.message: Walk with a friend at a pace where you can talk but not sing. You'll keep each other going a bit faster than you'd go alone.
ideas.why: A walking partner helps you keep a brisker pace.

ideas.title: A livelier ride
ideas.message: On your next ride, add a stretch where you pedal harder, up a hill or into the wind, until you're breathing hard, then ease off.
ideas.why: Harder stretches on a ride are a simple next step.

ideas.title: A few faster laps
ideas.message: In the pool, swim a faster lap between your usual easy ones, and see how it feels.
ideas.why: Faster laps between easy ones are a simple next step.

ideas.title: Dance it up
ideas.message: Put on a fast song and dance hard enough that you're breathing quicker. A few songs in a row makes a great workout.
ideas.why: Fast songs turn dancing into a lively workout.

ideas.title: The big garden jobs
ideas.message: Take on a bigger garden job like digging, pushing a hand mower or hauling mulch. Heavy garden work counts as vigorous activity.
ideas.why: Heavy garden work counts as vigorous activity.

ideas.title: Mix it up
ideas.message: To keep it fun, swap in something new now and then, like a new walking route, a swim or a dance class.
ideas.why: You're already active, so keep doing what works.

ideas.title: Strong and active
ideas.message: Alongside what you do, the guidelines also suggest muscle-strengthening moves on two days a week, like carrying groceries, heavy gardening or resistance bands.
ideas.why: Strength moves round out the activity you already do.

ideas.title: Bring someone along
ideas.message: Invite a friend or neighbor to join you now and then. You'll keep your routine going, and you might get them moving too.
ideas.why: Sharing what you do helps you keep it going.

ideas.title: Pass it on
ideas.message: Bring the grandkids along for a walk, a swim or a game in the park. You're passing on a great habit.
ideas.why: Being active with family passes on a great habit.

ideas.title: Add a little balance
ideas.message: The guidelines for older adults also suggest balance activities, like standing on one foot while you hold the kitchen counter, or walking heel to toe along the hall.
ideas.why: Balance practice rounds out the activity you already do.

ideas.title: Listen to your body
ideas.message: Keep an easy day in your week, and switch activities if something starts to ache. Staying steady matters as much as anything.
ideas.why: You're already active, so keep doing what works.

ideas.title: You and your dog
ideas.message: You and your dog have a great routine going. Keep enjoying those walks together.
ideas.why: You and your dog have a routine that works.

ideas.title: Notice your streak
ideas.message: Mark each active day on a calendar or in your phone. A row of check marks is a nice reminder of how far you've come.
ideas.why: Your streak is a nice reminder of what you do.

ideas.title: A regular bedtime
ideas.message: You could try a regular bedtime that leaves room for 7 hours, which CDC suggests for adults.
ideas.why: A regular bedtime leaves room for enough sleep.

ideas.title: A wind-down ritual
ideas.message: Give yourself a half-hour wind-down before bed: dim the lights, have a warm shower, read a few pages or play some quiet music. The same routine each night tells your body it's time to sleep.
ideas.why: A calm routine tells your body it's bedtime.

ideas.title: Morning daylight
ideas.message: Get outside into daylight soon after you wake, even for a few minutes with your coffee on the porch or on a short stroll. Morning light helps set your body clock.
ideas.why: Morning light helps set your body clock.

ideas.title: A fixed wake time
ideas.message: Get up at the same time every day, weekends too. A steady wake time makes it easier to feel sleepy at a regular hour at night.
ideas.why: A steady wake time helps you feel sleepy on time.

ideas.title: Screens off early
ideas.message: Put phones, laptops and the TV away about half an hour before bed, and charge your phone outside the bedroom if you can.
ideas.why: Screens off before bed make it easier to drift off.

ideas.title: A dark, quiet room
ideas.message: Make your bedroom dark, quiet and a little cool. Blackout curtains, an eye mask, or a fan for steady background sound can all help.
ideas.why: A dark, quiet, cool room makes it easier to sleep.

ideas.title: Park your worries
ideas.message: If your mind races at night, write down what's on it before bed, with one small next step for each. Then it's on paper, not on repeat.
ideas.why: Writing worries down can quiet a busy mind at bedtime.

ideas.title: A bedtime alarm
ideas.message: Set an alarm for bedtime, not just for waking. When it goes off, start winding down, even if it's in the middle of a show.
ideas.why: A reminder at bedtime helps you keep a regular schedule.

ideas.title: Short, early naps
ideas.message: If you nap, keep it short and before mid-afternoon, so you're still sleepy at bedtime.
ideas.why: Short, early naps leave you ready to sleep at night.

ideas.title: Move in the daytime
ideas.message: Being active during the day, like a walk in the afternoon, can make it easier to fall asleep at night. Just finish brisk exercise a few hours before bed.
ideas.why: Daytime activity can make it easier to fall asleep.

ideas.title: An earlier supper
ideas.message: Have your bigger meal earlier in the evening and skip alcohol close to bedtime, so your body can settle for sleep.
ideas.why: A lighter evening helps your body settle for sleep.

ideas.title: Bed is for sleep
ideas.message: If you can't fall asleep after a while, get up, do something calm in dim light, and go back to bed when you feel sleepy.
ideas.why: Keeping bed for sleep helps your body link them.

ideas.title: Stand for the ads
ideas.message: Each time the ads come on, stand up and move around the room until your show is back. Over an evening, it adds up.
ideas.why: Standing for each ad break breaks up long sitting.

ideas.title: Remote across the room
ideas.message: Keep the TV remote across the room, so changing the channel means a few steps each time.
ideas.why: A few extra steps each time break up long sitting.

ideas.title: Pace during phone calls
ideas.message: Whenever the phone rings, stand up and walk around while you talk. Long chats become easy movement.
ideas.why: Moving while you talk turns sitting time into moving time.

ideas.title: Stretch every chapter
ideas.message: At the end of each chapter, stand and stretch, or walk to the kitchen for a glass of water.
ideas.why: A stretch at each chapter breaks up long reading spells.

ideas.title: Stretch stops
ideas.message: On longer drives, plan a stop every hour or so to get out, walk around the car and stretch your legs.
ideas.why: Regular stops break up long drives.

ideas.title: A desk timer
ideas.message: At the computer, set a timer to stand up and walk around every half hour or so. Refill your water, or walk over to someone instead of sending a message.
ideas.why: Standing up regularly breaks up long sitting at a desk.

ideas.title: A walk between puzzles
ideas.message: Between puzzles or games, get up for a short walk around the house or out to the garden and back.
ideas.why: A short walk between puzzles breaks up long sitting.

ideas.title: Stand while it brews
ideas.message: Every time you make a cup of tea or coffee, stay on your feet while it brews: stretch your calves, roll your shoulders, look out of the window.
ideas.why: Small standing moments across the day break up sitting.

ideas.title: Shift and reach
ideas.message: Every hour, change position, sit up tall, and reach both arms overhead and out to the sides a few times. Small moves break up long spells of stillness.
ideas.why: Small moves in your seat break up stillness.

ideas.title: Stand in meetings
ideas.message: Stand for part of a video call or a meeting, or suggest a walking meeting with a colleague.
ideas.why: Standing for part of the work day breaks up sitting.

ideas.title: Up every hour
ideas.message: You could try standing up and moving for a few minutes every hour. Moving more and sitting less is good advice for everyone.
ideas.why: Standing up more often breaks up long sitting.

ideas.title: Spread out the chores
ideas.message: Instead of doing chores all at once, spread them through the day: fold some laundry, water the plants or put the dishes away between sitting spells.
ideas.why: Chores spread through the day break up sitting.

ideas.title: A show-time stretch
ideas.message: During each show, do a few seated stretches: stretch and flex your feet, circle your ankles and roll your shoulders.
ideas.why: Moving in your seat breaks up long sitting.

limitations: Suggestions follow public-health guidance and the model's lever ranking; they are not medical advice and promise no benefit.
The model compares similar people over one to five years; it does not show what a change would do for you.
The server keeps nothing. Habit notes and history stay on your phone.

chair_march.title: Chair marching
chair_march.steps: Sit tall in a sturdy chair and march your feet in place for {minutes} minutes. Swing your arms too, if that feels good.
source: NIA: Exercise and physical activity for older adults

seated_leg_lifts.title: Seated leg lifts
seated_leg_lifts.steps: Sit in a sturdy chair. Slowly straighten one knee, then lower it, and switch legs, for {minutes} minutes.

seated_arm_raises.title: Seated arm raises
seated_arm_raises.steps: Sitting in a chair, raise both arms out to the sides and lower them slowly, for {minutes} minutes. Two water bottles make good light weights.
source: CDC: What counts as physical activity for older adults

seated_dance.title: Dancing in your chair
seated_dance.steps: Put on a song you love and dance from your chair for {minutes} minutes: arms, shoulders and feet.
source: CDC: What counts as physical activity for older adults

stationary_bike.title: Easy exercise bike
stationary_bike.steps: Pedal an exercise bike at an easy pace for {minutes} minutes. It is gentle on the knees.

water_walk.title: Walking in the pool
water_walk.steps: Walk back and forth in the shallow end of a pool for {minutes} minutes. The water is gentle on sore joints.
source: CDC: What counts as physical activity for older adults

walk_short.title: A short, flat walk
walk_short.steps: Take a {minutes}-minute walk on flat ground, at a pace where you can still talk.
source: CDC: Physical activity guidelines for older adults

walk_brisk.title: A brisk walk
walk_brisk.steps: Walk at a brisk pace for {minutes} minutes, quick enough that talking takes a little effort.
source: CDC: Physical activity guidelines for older adults

hill_walk.title: A hill walk or swimming laps
hill_walk.steps: Walk briskly up a gentle hill, or swim laps, for {minutes} minutes, hard enough that you can only say a few words at a time.
source: CDC: Physical activity guidelines for older adults

sit_to_stand.title: Sit-to-stand
sit_to_stand.steps: From a sturdy chair, stand up slowly and sit back down, using the armrests if you need them. Repeat for {minutes} minutes, resting whenever you like.
source: NIA: Exercise and physical activity for older adults

wall_pushups.title: Wall push-ups
wall_pushups.steps: Stand an arm's length from a wall with your hands on it, and slowly bend and straighten your arms for {minutes} minutes.
source: CDC: What counts as physical activity for older adults

heel_raises.title: Heel raises, holding the counter
heel_raises.steps: Hold a kitchen counter with both hands. Rise up onto your toes and lower slowly, for {minutes} minutes.
source: NIA: Exercise and physical activity for older adults

tandem_stand.title: Heel-to-toe stand, holding the counter
tandem_stand.steps: Hold a kitchen counter. Stand with one foot right in front of the other, heel to toe, then switch feet, for {minutes} minutes.
source: USPSTF 2024: exercise to prevent falls in older adults (AAFP summary)

one_leg_stand.title: One-leg stand
one_leg_stand.steps: Stand on one foot next to a counter, then switch feet, for {minutes} minutes. Touch the counter whenever you need to.
source: CDC: Physical activity guidelines for older adults

tai_chi.title: Gentle tai chi
tai_chi.steps: Follow a gentle tai chi class or video for {minutes} minutes, moving slowly.
source: CDC STEADI programmes, including Tai Chi: Moving for Better Balance

gardening.title: Gardening
gardening.steps: Spend {minutes} minutes in the garden: weeding, raking or watering. A stool or raised bed helps.
source: CDC: What counts as physical activity for older adults

dancing.title: Dancing to music
dancing.steps: Put on music you love and dance around the kitchen for {minutes} minutes.
source: CDC: What counts as physical activity for older adults

jog_walk.title: A brisk walk or jog
jog_walk.steps: Walk briskly, or jog if you like, for {minutes} minutes, at a pace where you can still talk in short sentences.
source: CDC: Physical activity guidelines for adults

bodyweight_circuit.title: A bodyweight circuit
bodyweight_circuit.steps: Go round squats, lunges, push-ups and a plank, about a minute each, for {minutes} minutes. Rest when you need to.
source: CDC: Physical activity guidelines for adults

cycling.title: Cycling
cycling.steps: Ride a bike at a steady pace for {minutes} minutes, to somewhere you need to go or just for fun.
source: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64

sport_friends.title: A sport with friends
sport_friends.steps: Play a sport you enjoy with friends for {minutes} minutes: football, basketball, tennis or anything that gets you moving.
source: CDC: Physical activity guidelines for adults

stairs.title: Take the stairs
stairs.steps: Climb up and down a flight of stairs at a steady pace for {minutes} minutes, or take the stairs instead of the lift today.
source: CDC: Physical activity guidelines for adults

swim_laps.title: Swimming
swim_laps.steps: Swim at a steady pace for {minutes} minutes, resting at the wall whenever you like.
source: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64

strength_twice.title: Strength work
strength_twice.steps: Do squats, lunges, a plank and rows with a backpack or a band for {minutes} minutes. Two days a week is a good rhythm.
source: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64

mobility_flow.title: Mobility and stretching
mobility_flow.steps: Sit tall on a chair or a mat and slowly move your neck, shoulders, back and hips through their range for {minutes} minutes.
source: NHS: Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64

protein_each_meal.title: Some protein at each meal
protein_each_meal.message: Try adding some protein to each meal, like eggs, beans, yogurt or fish. If your doctor has told you to limit protein, follow that.
protein_each_meal.why: Many older adults don't get enough protein, and it helps keep muscles strong.
source: ACL: Nutrition needs of older adults, protein

younger.why: Most people do well with some protein at each meal, and it helps keep muscles strong.

fluids.title: Sip water through the day
fluids.message: Keep a glass of water nearby and sip through the day, before you feel thirsty, unless your doctor limits your fluids.
fluids.why: Thirst fades with age, so it helps to drink before you feel thirsty.
source: NIA: Healthy meal planning tips for older adults

younger.why: Most people feel better when they drink water regularly through the day.
source: NHS: Water, drinks and your health

dash_less_salt.title: Go easy on salt
dash_less_salt.message: Taste your food before adding salt, and pick lower-salt soups and sauces when you can.
dash_less_salt.why: Less salt and a DASH-style way of eating help keep blood pressure down.

mediterranean.title: Mediterranean-style meals
mediterranean.message: Build a meal around vegetables, beans, olive oil and fish, the Mediterranean way.
mediterranean.why: A Mediterranean pattern of eating is linked with heart health in large studies.
source: Harvard Nutrition Source: the PREDIMED republication

fiber.title: A little more fiber
fiber.message: Add a fruit, a vegetable, or a whole grain like oats or beans to one meal today.
fiber.why: Fruit, vegetables and whole grains are the heart of healthy eating for older adults.
source: NIA: Healthy meal planning tips for older adults

younger.why: Most people eat less fiber than they could, and fruit, vegetables and whole grains are the heart of healthy eating.

care_team_food.title: Food questions with diabetes
care_team_food.message: With diabetes, your care team or a dietitian is the best guide for food choices. Medicare Part B covers medical nutrition therapy with a dietitian for diabetes or kidney disease, when your doctor refers you.
care_team_food.why: Food needs with diabetes are different for each person, so they belong with your care team.

younger.message: With diabetes, your care team or a dietitian is the best guide for food choices. Your doctor can refer you to a dietitian.
source: NIDDK: Diet, eating and physical activity with diabetes

care_team_kidney.title: Food questions with kidney disease
care_team_kidney.message: With kidney disease, please ask your kidney doctor or a dietitian before changing how much protein or fluid you have. Medicare Part B covers medical nutrition therapy with a dietitian for kidney disease, when your doctor refers you.
care_team_kidney.why: Protein and fluid needs with kidney disease are different for each person.

younger.message: With kidney disease, please ask your kidney doctor or a dietitian before changing how much protein or fluid you have. Your doctor can refer you to a dietitian.
source: NIDDK: Eating and nutrition for chronic kidney disease

quit_help.title: Help with smoking, if you want it
quit_help.message: If you'd like help to quit smoking, your doctor or a free quit line can help. Want me to remind you to ask?
quit_help.why: Quitting is the change the model ranks first, at any age.

sleep_routine.title: A steady bedtime
sleep_routine.message: Try going to bed and getting up at the same time each day, and get some daylight in the morning.
sleep_routine.why: You've been sleeping under seven hours, and a steady routine helps sleep.

sitting_breaks.title: Up during the ad breaks
sitting_breaks.message: When an ad comes on, stand up and move around until the show is back.
sitting_breaks.why: Breaking up long sitting is good for everyone, whatever else you do.
source: WHO 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour

variants.seated_only: When an ad comes on, shift in your chair, stretch your arms up and roll your shoulders until the show is back.

replies.SUPPLEMENT_REPLY: I don't suggest supplements, because they can mix badly with medicines. A pharmacist can check them for free: bring your bottles to your pharmacist or your doctor next time.
replies.MEDICINE_REPLY: Please don't change your medicines without your doctor. Your doctor or pharmacist is the right person for that question.
replies.DIAGNOSIS_REPLY: I can't tell what that is. Please check with your doctor soon.
replies.WEIGHT_REPLY: I don't give weight-loss plans. If your weight is on your mind, your doctor is the best person to ask. Here's a food idea instead.
replies.DIABETES_FOOD_REPLY: For food questions with diabetes, your care team or a dietitian is the best guide. Medicare covers medical nutrition therapy for diabetes, when your doctor refers you.
replies.KIDNEY_FOOD_REPLY: With kidney disease, please ask your kidney doctor or a dietitian about protein and fluids. Medicare covers medical nutrition therapy for kidney disease, when your doctor refers you.
replies.FORECAST_REPLY: Nobody can tell how long a person will live, and I never guess. The model only compares similar people over the next one to five years, and it shows links, not causes.
replies.BP_CRISIS_REPLY: That blood pressure reading is very high. Sit quietly for a few minutes and check it again. If it is still that high, please contact your doctor now. Call 911 if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, a change in vision or trouble speaking.
replies.RED_FLAG_REPLY: Let's pause movement ideas for now. Please check with your doctor before trying them again.
replies.CLEARED_REPLY: That's good news. We'll start small again.
